Avoiding intersections of given size in finite affine spaces AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2)

Benedek Kovács ††thanks: ELTE Linear Hypergraphs Research Group, Eötvös Loránd University, Budapest, Hungary. The author is supported by the ÚNKP-23-3 New National Excellence Program of the Ministry for Culture and Innovation from the source of the National Research, Development and Innovation Fund. E-mail: benoke98@student.elte.hu    Zoltán Lóránt Nagy ††thanks: ELTE Linear Hypergraphs Research Group, Eötvös Loránd University, Budapest, Hungary. The author is supported by the Hungarian Research Grant (NKFIH) No. PD 134953. and No. K. 124950. E-mail: nagyzoli@cs.elte.hu
Abstract

We study the set of intersection sizes of a kk-dimensional affine subspace and a point set of size m∈[0,2n]m\in[0,2^{n}] of the nn-dimensional binary affine space AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2). Following the theme of Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós, we partially determine which local densities in kk-dimensional affine subspaces are unavoidable in all mm-element point sets in the nn-dimensional affine space.
We also show constructions of point sets for which the intersection sizes with kk-dimensional affine subspaces takes values from a set of a small size compared to 2k2^{k}. These are built up from affine subspaces and so-called subspace evasive sets. Meanwhile, we improve the best known upper bounds on subspace evasive sets and apply results concerning the canonical signed-digit (CSD) representation of numbers.
Keywords: unavoidable, affine subspaces, evasive sets, random methods, canonical signed-digit number system.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we address the following general problem. Let SS be a subset of size mm of the affine space AG⁡(n,q)\mathrm{AG}(n,q). Does there always exist a kk-dimensional affine subspace which contains exactly tt points of SS? A kk-dimensional affine subspace will be referred to as a kk-flat, and a kk-flat which contains exactly tt points of a given set SS will be called a [k,t][k,t]-flat (induced by SS). If for every mm-element set SS in the nn-dimensional affine space, there is a kk-flat containing exactly tt points of SS, then we say that the pair [n,m][n,m] forces the pair [k,t][k,t], or that tt-sets are unavoidable in kk-flats. We use the notation [n,m]q→[k,t][n,m]_{q}\rightarrow[k,t] for this concept.

Our main focus will be the case q=2q=2, and we will omit the index qq except when we wish to refer to arbitrary finite fields.

The graph theoretic analogue of this problem was initiated by Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós [11].

Let G⁡(n,m)G(n,m) denote a graph on nn vertices and mm edges. Fix a positive integer kk and a pair of integers (n,m)(n,m) such that 0≤m≤(n2)0\leq m\leq\binom{n}{2}. For which tt does it hold that any nn-vertex graph with mm edges contains an induced subgraph on kk vertices having exactly tt edges? Equivalently, we are seeking pairs (k,t)(k,t) such that kk-vertex induced subgraphs with tt edges are unavoidable in graphs of the form G⁡(n,m)G(n,m). Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós introduced the notation (n,m)→(k,t)(n,m)\rightarrow(k,t) for the case when this is true.

Their main result showed that forced pairs (k,t)(k,t) are rare in the following sense. Consider the set S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) of all edge cardinalities mm such that (n,m)→(k,t)(n,m)\rightarrow(k,t). Its density is the ratio |S​p​(n,k,t)|(n2)\frac{|Sp(n;k,t)|}{\binom{n}{2}}. They proved that the limit superior of this density is bounded from above by 2/32/3 apart from a handful cases, and is 00 for the majority of the pairs (k,t)(k,t) for fixed and large enough kk. Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós conjectured that in fact it is bounded from above by 1/21/2 apart from finitely many pairs (k,t)(k,t). This was confirmed recently by He, Ma and Zhao [17]. Several related problems have been studied in the last couple of years [1, 2, 7].

Our problem can be viewed as the qq-analogue of this problem, in which we investigate whether all subspaces of given dimension kk can avoid to have an intersection of size tt with an mm-element set of the space AG⁡(n,q)\mathrm{AG}(n,q), which corresponds to 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}.

Note that problems of similar flavour have gained significant interest in the past and are trending as well in recent years. The celebrated Sylvester-Gallai theorem showed that if a set of mm points in the Euclidean 22-dimensional space is not collinear, then there will be a line which intersects the point set in exactly 22 points.
Considering the case q=3q=3, k=1k=1 and t=3t=3, we in turn get the famous cap set problem, which asks for the maximum number of points in AG⁡(n,3)\mathrm{AG}(n,3) without creating a line, or in other words, without containing a 33-term arithmetic progression. There has been a recent breakthrough due to Ellenberg and Gijswijt [10], building upon the ideas of Croot, Lev and Pach [9], which showed that to avoid complete lines, |S|/3n|S|/3^{n} has to be exponentially small. The arithmetic removal lemma implies a supersaturation result on the number of complete lines [14], from which bounds on the case [1,3][1,3] translate to similar bounds for the case of complete kk-flats, i.e., cases [k,3k][k,3^{k}]. This connection highlights the complexity of the problem.

There has been significant interest in the case when we want to forbid each intersection of size larger than or equal to tt instead of avoiding only tt-sets in kk-flats. If there exists a set S⊆AG⁡(n,q)S\subseteq\mathrm{AG}(n,q) for which all kk-dimensional affine subspaces contain at most cc points of SS, then SS is called (k,c)(k,c)-subspace evasive. The importance of such sets is highlighted by its connections to explicit constructions of bipartite Ramsey graphs by Pudlák and Rödl [23] and to list-decodable codes by Guruswami [15].

By a standard application of the first moment method, Guruswami obtained random subsets of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n} of large size which are (k,c)(k,c)-subspace evasive. (Here and throughout the paper, 𝔽\mathbb{F} denotes a finite field.)

Theorem 1.1 (Guruswami, [15]).

For any fixed pair (k,c)(k,c), there exists a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set in 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n} of size at least C⋅|𝔽|n⁡(1−2​kc)C\cdot|\mathbb{F}|^{n(1-\frac{2k}{c})}, where C>0C>0 is a constant independent of nn.

Corollary 1.2.

For any fixed pair (k,t)(k,t) with t>1t>1, there exists a constant C>0C>0 for which the following holds: if m≤C⋅2n⁡(1−2​kt−1)m\leq C\cdot 2^{n(1-\frac{2k}{t-1})}, then tt-sets are avoidable in the kk-flats of AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2), i.e., in this case [n,m]↛[k,t][n,m]\not\rightarrow[k,t].

Surprisingly it turned out that the obtained bounds are sharp in a weak sense. Improving the results of Ben-Aroya and Shinkar [3], Sudakov and Tomon proved the following.

Theorem 1.3 (Sudakov and Tomon, [25]).

Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be a field, k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} and ε∈(0,0.05)\varepsilon\in(0,0.05). If nn is sufficiently large with respect to kk, and S⊆𝔽nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}^{n} has size m≥|𝔽|n⁡(1−ε)m\geq|\mathbb{F}|^{n(1-\varepsilon)}, then SS is not (k,k−log2⁡(1/ε)8​ε)(k,\frac{k-\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{8\varepsilon})-subspace evasive.

Note however that SS being non-(k,c)(k,c)-evasive does not necessarily imply that SS contains a kk-flat with c+1c+1 points, except when c=|𝔽|n−1.c=|\mathbb{F}|^{n}-1. The latter case on the other hand is not covered by the theorem, as k−log2⁡(1/ε)8​ε<2k−3\frac{k-\log_{2}(1/\varepsilon)}{8\varepsilon}<2^{k-3} holds for every ε∈(0,0.05)\varepsilon\in(0,0.05).

1.1 Our main results

Similarly to the investigation in [11], we define the set of forcing sizes mm with respect to [k,t][k,t], which are the sizes for which a [k,t][k,t]-flat is unavoidable, as follows.

Definition 1.4.
S​p​(n,k,t):={m:[n,m]q→[k,t]}Sp(n;k,t):=\{m:[n,m]_{q}\rightarrow[k,t]\}

is called the set of forcing sizes with respect to n,k,tn,k,t, and we refer to it as the (n,k,t)(n;k,t)-spectrum.

ρ⁡(n,k,t):=|S​p​(n,k,t)||𝔽|n\rho(n;k,t):=\frac{|Sp(n;k,t)|}{|\mathbb{F}|^{n}}

is the density of the spectrum.

(We will always assume that k≤nk\leq n, even if it is not specifically mentioned.)

Our aim is to characterize the spectra or at least bound the density of the spectra for various values of kk and tt. Note that from now on, 𝔽\mathbb{F} is considered to be the binary field.

In their paper [11], Erdős, Füredi, Rothschild and T. Sós construct some graph families which only induce kk-vertex subgraphs of specific sizes. These families are the combination of graphs which are very dense (cliques, or graphs close to cliques in edit distance) and sparse graphs (forests, or graphs with high girth).

In that aspect, we follow their footsteps and provide point sets which are combinations of disjoint full flats and point sets which hit every kk-flat in only a small number of points.

These constructions show that the binary representation of mm and tt will be key in our results concerning sizes mm not in the spectrum.

Theorem 1.5.

If 0<t<2k0<t<2^{k} then S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) will not contain those values m<2nm<2^{n} which have fewer 11-digits than the number of 11-digits of tt in the binary representation, denoted by s2​(t)s_{2}(t). Since S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) cannot contain 2n2^{n} either, this means that at least

1+∑i=0s2​(t)−1(ni)1+\sum_{i=0}^{s_{2}(t)-1}\binom{n}{i}

values are missing from the (n,k,t)(n;k,t)-spectrum.

In fact, another numeral system, the so-called canonical signed-digit binary representation of integers will also have a central role. We formulate the corresponding Proposition 3.10 in Section 3, which is the analogue of Theorem 1.5.

These results can be combined with the former results on (k,c)(k,c)-subspace evasive sets. Indeed, if we take a point set S0S_{0} which avoids kk-dimensional subspaces having intersection of size rr for all r∈[t1,t2]r\in[t_{1},t_{2}] with c≤t2−t1c\leq t_{2}-t_{1}, then the union of S0S_{0} and a (k,c)(k,c)-subspace evasive set S1S_{1} will avoid kk-dimensional subspaces with intersections of size t∈[t1+c,t2]t\in[t_{1}+c,t_{2}].

As we have seen in Corollary 1.2, subsets of large evasive sets provide point sets of various sizes which do not induce [k,t][k,t]-flats for large enough tt. We improve upon the probabilistic construction of Guruswami in order to obtain larger point sets and to apply the result for every t≥k+1t\geq k+1.

Theorem 1.6 (General improved lower bound on evasive sets).

Let k,c∈ℤ+k,c\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} with c≥k+1c\geq k+1. Then for n>kn>k, there exists a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} of size at least

K⋅qn⁡(1−kc)K\cdot q^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}

for some constant KK independent of nn.

The combination of these yields long intervals of missing values from the spectrum S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t).

Theorem 1.7.

Let kk and tt be fixed integers such that 1≤t≤2k−11\leq t\leq 2^{k}-1 and suppose that the difference between the number of nonzero digits of tt and mm is greater than ⌈12​(log2⁡c+1)⌉\left\lceil\frac{1}{2}\left(\log_{2}c+1\right)\right\rceil for some positive integers mm and cc in the so-called canonical signed-digit binary representation. Then [n,m′]↛[k,t][n,m^{\prime}]\not\to[k,t] holds for every m′∈[m−(K⋅m2n⋅2n⁡(1−kc)),m+(K⋅2n−m2n⋅2n⁡(1−kc))]m^{\prime}\in\left[m-\left(K\cdot\frac{m}{2^{n}}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\right),m+\left(K\cdot\frac{2^{n}-m}{2^{n}}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\right)\right], where KK is a positive constant depending only on kk and cc.

Our next goal is to prove results on long intervals the spectrum S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) must contain for certain special values of tt. Our first results in this direction concern the case when tt is a power of 22.

Theorem 1.8.

Suppose that k>ℓ≥1k>\ell\geq 1 are integers. Then there exist constants C>0C>0 and 0<D<10<D<1 depending on k,ℓk,\ell such that [n,m]→[k,2k−ℓ][n,m]\rightarrow\left[k,2^{k-\ell}\right] for m∈[C⋅2n⁡(1−12k−ℓ−1),D⋅2n]m\in\left[C\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-\ell-1}}\right)},D\cdot 2^{n}\right]. Moreover, for each ε>0\varepsilon>0 and sufficiently large nn,

ρ⁡(n,k,2k−ℓ)≥1−ε2ℓ−1.\rho(n;k,2^{k-\ell})\geq\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2^{\ell-1}}.

As for the case ℓ=0\ell=0, it can be shown analogously to the proof of Szemerédi’s Cube Lemma (see [26, Corollary 2.1]) that in order for a set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} to induce a [k,2k][k,2^{k}]-flat, it suffices for |S|2n\frac{|S|}{2^{n}} to be exponentially small, and so limn→∞ρ⁡(n,k,2k)=1\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n;k,2^{k})=1. For ℓ=1\ell=1, Theorem 1.8 implies that limn→∞ρ⁡(n,k,2k−1)=1\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n;k,2^{k-1})=1 holds as well, and we have an even stronger result in this case:

Theorem 1.9.

Let k≥2k\geq 2. Then there exists a constant C>0C>0 depending on kk such that [n,m]→[k,2k−1][n,m]~\rightarrow~\left[k,2^{k-1}\right] for m∈[C⋅2n⁡(1−12k−2),2n−C⋅2n⁡(1−12k−2)]m\in\left[C\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)},2^{n}-C\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)}\right].

A work closely related to the case of full flats (ℓ=0\ell=0) is due to Etzion and Vardy [12], who determined the minimal number of points needed in AG⁡(n,2)\mathrm{AG}(n,2) (and in general in AG⁡(n,q)\mathrm{AG}(n,q)) in order to cover each subspace of a given dimension kk, under the name of qq-Turán designs 𝒯q​(n,k,1)\mathcal{T}_{q}(n,k,1). Their result 𝒯q​(n,k,1)=qn−k+1−1q−1\mathcal{T}_{q}(n,k,1)=\frac{q^{n-k+1}-1}{q-1} highlights how much harder it is to avoid a complete kk-flat in our affine variant compared to theirs.

As we have seen, if tt is not a power of 22, then we must expect that the spectrum is scattered, several values of mm are missing from it.

For k≤2k\leq 2 we have complete characterizations of the spectra, except for the case [k,t]=[2,4][k,t]=[2,4] which corresponds to Sidon sets of binary spaces. We present the characterization and discuss the results related to the exceptional case in Section 2.

Finally, we discuss a case when tt is the sum of two consecutive powers of 22. This case is significantly more involved compared to the case of t=2k−ℓt=2^{k-\ell}.

Theorem 1.10.

For every pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) of integers with 2≤ℓ≤k−12\leq\ell\leq k-1, the density of integer values mm within the interval [0,12ℓ−1⋅2n]\left[0,\frac{1}{2^{\ell-1}}\cdot 2^{n}\right] for which [n,m]→[k,3⋅2k−ℓ][n,m]\to[k,3\cdot 2^{k-\ell}] holds, tends to 11 as n→∞n\to\infty. Hence ρ⁡(n,k,3⋅2k−ℓ)≥12ℓ−1.\rho(n;k,3\cdot 2^{k-\ell})\geq\frac{1}{2^{\ell-1}}.

In general, we have the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.11.
limn→∞ρ⁡(n,k,t)=1.\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho(n;k,t)=1.

The paper is organized as follows: in Section 2 we present notations and some tools we will use, then discuss the cases when kk is small. In Section 3 we refine the probabilistic bound of Guruswami and prove Theorem 1.6. We continue by collecting the results on sizes mm for which [k,t][k,t]-flats are avoidable. We discuss the case when tt is a power of 22 in Section 4, and present the proof of Theorem 1.8 and 1.9. Then we relate the additive energy of a set SS with the number of [2,3][2,3]-flats induced by SS in Section 5. We prove bounds on the additive energy via good estimates on the size of certain cuts in hypercube graphs, which enables us to derive Theorem 1.10. Finally, the last section is devoted to concluding remarks and open problems.

2 Preliminaries, small cases for kk

2.1 Notations and tools

For a pair of integers a≤ba\leq b, [a,b][a,b] will be used to refer to the set {a,a+1,…,b}⊆ℤ\{a,a+1,...,b\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}. We use the standard additive combinatorial notation for the sumset A+BA+B of two subsets AA and BB of an abelian group GG as the set of all sums of an element from AA with an element from BB, i.e., A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B}A+B=\{a+b:a\in A,b\in B\}. A−BA-B is defined similarly. If one of the sets consists of a single element, we omit the brackets for short.
The complement of a set SS will be denoted by S¯\overline{S}.

It will be useful to define the kk-dimensional profile pfk​(L)\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L) of a set L⊆𝔽2nL\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} as the set of all possible intersection sizes of LL and a kk-flat of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. Thus we have that t∉pfk​(L)t\not\in\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L) implies |L|∉S​p​(n,k,t)|L|\not\in Sp(n;k,t). We show a simple but useful lemma concerning the kk-dimensional profiles.

Lemma 2.1.

  1. (i)

    Suppose that L1,L2⊆𝔽2nL_{1},L_{2}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} are disjoint sets. Then pfk​(L1∪L2)⊆pfk​(L1)+pfk​(L2)\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{1}\cup L_{2})\subseteq\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{1})+\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{2}).

  2. (ii)

    Suppose that L1⊆L2⊆𝔽2nL_{1}\subseteq L_{2}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. Then pfk​(L2∖L1)⊆pfk​(L2)−pfk​(L1)\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{2}\setminus L_{1})\subseteq\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{2})-\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{1}).

Proof.

These immediately follow from the fact that for any kk-flat HH, |H∩Li|∈pfk​(Li)|H\cap L_{i}|\in\mathrm{pf}_{k}(L_{i}). ∎

The next lemma will be useful for inductive arguments.

Lemma 2.2 (Charbit et al., [8]).

Given any subset S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of size mm, there exists a linear subspace H≤𝔽2nH\leq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of dimension n−1n-1 such that |H∩S|∈[12​m−12​m,12​m+12​m]|H\cap S|\in\left[\frac{1}{2}m-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{m},\frac{1}{2}m+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{m}\right].

In order to apply bounds on the number of certain affine subspaces, important ingredients will be the Gaussian binomials and their estimates.

Definition 2.3.

[nk]q\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q} denotes the number of kk-dimensional subspaces of an nn-dimensional vector space over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

Corollary 2.4.

qn−k​[nk]qq^{n-k}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q} is the number of kk-flats in AG⁡(n,q).\mathrm{AG}(n,q).

We will apply bounds on these Gaussian binomials, i.e. on the number of subspaces. As it was proved in [18], we have

Lemma 2.5 (Héger, Nagy, [18]).

[nk]2<2(n−k)​k+1⋅e2/3\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{2}<2^{(n-k)k+1}\cdot e^{2/3} and [nk]q<q(n−k)​k⋅e1/(q−2)\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q}<q^{(n-k)k}\cdot e^{1/(q-2)} for q>2q>2 and k>0k>0.

We will also use the so-called Euler function ϕ⁡(q)=∏k=1∞(1−qk)\phi(q)=\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}(1-q^{k}) where q∈ℂq\in\mathbb{C}, |q|<1|q|<1.

For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and any set A⊆VA\subseteq V, e⁡(A)e(A) denotes the number of edges spanned by AA, and if AA and BB are disjoint subsets of VV then e⁡(A,B)e(A,B) denotes the number of edges between AA and BB.

2.2 Small cases

We will first investigate S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) in cases where kk is small. Firstly, we can see that determining the spectrum S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t), or its density, is essentially the same problem as determining S​p​(n,k,2k−t)Sp(n;k,2^{k}-t), or its density:

Lemma 2.6.

If n,k≥1n,k\geq 1 are integers and 0≤t≤2k0\leq t\leq 2^{k}, then S​p​(n,k,t)=2n−S​p​(n,k,2k−t)Sp(n;k,t)=2^{n}-Sp(n;k,2^{k}-t).

Proof.

Suppose m∈S​p​(n,k,t)m\in Sp(n;k,t). Now take any set T⊆𝔽2nT\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} with |T|=2n−m|T|=2^{n}-m. Then T¯\overline{T} is a set of size mm, hence there exists a kk-flat FkF_{k} such that |T¯∩Fk|=t|\overline{T}\cap F_{k}|=t. Then |T∩Fk|=|Fk|−t=2k−t|T\cap F_{k}|=|F_{k}|-t=2^{k}-t, so TT induces a [k,2k−t][k,2^{k}-t]-flat. So 2n−m∈S​p​(n,k,2k−t)2^{n}-m\in Sp(n;k,2^{k}-t), meaning that m∈2n−S​p​(n,k,2k−t)m\in 2^{n}-Sp(n;k,2^{k}-t). The other containment can be seen by symmetry. ∎

Proposition 2.7.
  1. (i)

    S​p​(n,1,0)=[0,2n−2]Sp(n;1,0)=[0,2^{n}-2],

  2. (ii)

    S​p​(n,1,1)=[1,2n−1]Sp(n;1,1)=[1,2^{n}-1],

  3. (iii)

    S​p​(n,1,2)=[2,2n]Sp(n;1,2)=[2,2^{n}],

  4. (iv)

    S​p​(n,2,1)=[0,2n]∖({2n}∪{2n−2d:d∈[0,n]})Sp(n;2,1)=[0,2^{n}]\setminus(\{2^{n}\}\cup\{2^{n}-2^{d}:d\in[0,n]\}),

  5. (v)

    S​p​(n,2,2)=[2,2n−2]Sp(n;2,2)=[2,2^{n}-2],

  6. (vi)

    S​p​(n,2,3)=[0,2n]∖({0}∪{2d:d∈[0,n]})Sp(n;2,3)=[0,2^{n}]\setminus(\{0\}\cup\{2^{d}:d\in[0,n]\}).

Proof.

Consider part (i) first and observe that a [1,0][1,0]-flat consists of any two points outside SS, which in turn implies the claim. Similarly in part (iii), any two points in SS make a [1,2][1,2]-flat. For part (ii), a [1,1][1,1]-flat consists of any two points such that one of them is in SS and the other is not, so a set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} induces a [1,1][1,1]-flat if and only if 1≤|S|≤2n−11\leq|S|\leq 2^{n}-1.
For parts (iv) and (vi), a nonempty set SS induces a [2,3][2,3]-flat if and only if there exists x∈𝔽2nx\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} and nonzero a,b∈𝔽2na,b\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} such that x,x+a,x+b∈Sx,x+a,x+b\in S but x+a+b∉Sx+a+b\not\in S. This is exactly the condition such that SS is not an affine subspace of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, hence the sizes forcing a [2,3][2,3]-flat are exactly those which are not zero and not powers of 2. By applying Lemma 2.6, we also obtain the sizes forcing a [2,1][2,1]-flat.

For part (v), we can see that a [2,2][2,2]-flat needs at least two points in SS and at least two not in SS, so S​p​(n,2,2)⊆[2,2n−2]Sp(n;2,2)\subseteq[2,2^{n}-2]. On the other hand, if 2≤|S|≤2n−22\leq|S|\leq 2^{n}-2, then take a pair of points (s,s′)(s,s^{\prime}) with s∈Ss\in S and s′∉Ss^{\prime}\not\in S. Letting v=s′−sv=s^{\prime}-s, subdivide 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} into the pairs determined by the ⟨v⟩\langle v\rangle-cosets. Note that any two of the pairs form a 22-flat. Knowing that the pair {s,s′}\{s,s^{\prime}\} contains exactly one element of SS (i.e. is a [1,1][1,1]-flat), if we found another pair with exactly one element of SS then they together would form a [2,2][2,2]-flat. Assuming there is no other such pair, all other pairs must either be [1,2][1,2]- or [1,0][1,0]-flats. But a [1,2][1,2]-flat and a [1,0][1,0]-flat also form a [2,2][2,2]-flat together, so assuming this does not happen, either all other pairs are [1,2][1,2]-flats (in which case |S|=2n−1|S|=2^{n}-1), or all other flats are [1,0][1,0]-flats (in which case |S|=1|S|=1), giving a contradiction in both cases. ∎

The determination of the spectrum S​p​(n,2,4)Sp(n;2,4) (and its complement S​p​(n,2,0)Sp(n;2,0)) is still a challenging problem. This problem has been studied under the name of Sidon sets in binary vector spaces. A subset SS of an abelian group AA is a Sidon set if the only solutions to the equation a+b=c+da+b=c+d with a,b,c,d∈Aa,b,c,d\in A are the trivial solutions when (a,b)(a,b) is a permutation of (c,d)(c,d). Observe that for A=𝔽2nA=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, SS contains a [2,4][2,4]-flat if and only if it is not a Sidon set. There are known results on Sidon sets in this setting due to Bose, Ray-Chaudhuri, by Tait, Won and by Lindström, which imply the following.

Proposition 2.8.
  1. (i)

    ([6], also see [21, 27]) There exists a constant C>0C>0 such that [n,m]→[2,4][n,m]\to[2,4] for every m≥C⋅2n/2m\geq C\cdot 2^{n/2}.

  2. (ii)

    ([6]) For even nn, the explicit construction {(x,x3):x∈𝔽2n/2}\{(x,x^{3}):x\in\mathbb{F}_{2^{n/2}}\} shows that [n,2n/2]↛[2,4][n,2^{n/2}]\not\to[2,4].

The complete characterization of the spectrum for the case k=3k=3, t=4t=4 requires a combination of various tools, including probabilistic methods.

Proposition 2.9.

S​p​(n,3,4)=[4,2n−4]Sp(n;3,4)=[4,2^{n}-4].

Proof.

It is clear that a [3,4][3,4]-flat requires at least 4 points in SS and at least 4 not in SS, so S​p​(n,3,4)⊆[4,2n−4]Sp(n;3,4)\subseteq[4,2^{n}-4].

Firstly we show that in the case 4≤|S|≤2n−2−14\leq|S|\leq 2^{n-2}-1, SS induces a [3,4][3,4]-flat. Assume on the contrary that it does not. Consider the parallel classes of 22-flats. In any given parallel class, there must be at least one [2,0][2,0]-flat (otherwise SS would have at least 2n−22^{n-2} points). If the same class also contains a [2,4][2,4]-flat, then together with the [2,0][2,0]-flat they would form a [3,4][3,4]-flat, which is a contradiction. So SS cannot induce any [2,4][2,4]-flats at all. Take a line ℓ={a,b}\ell=\{a,b\} joining any two points of SS. The 22-flats through ℓ\ell cover each point outside ℓ\ell exactly once, and there cannot be a [2,4][2,4]-flat among them, so there must be at least one [2,3][2,3]-flat (since |S|≥3|S|\geq 3). Take any [2,3][2,3]-flat HH, and consider the parallel class of HH. If it contains any [2,1][2,1]-flat, then together with HH it would form a [3,4][3,4]-flat, which is a contradiction. So the class can only contain flats of type [2,0][2,0], [2,2][2,2] and [2,3][2,3]. There can be at most one [2,2][2,2]-flat, as two [2,2][2,2]-flats again form a [3,4][3,4]-flat. Now suppose H′H^{\prime} is another [2,3][2,3]-flat in this class. Let H={x,x+a,x+b,x+a+b}H=\{x,~x+a,~x+b,~x+a+b\} with x,x+a,x+b∈Sx,~x+a,~x+b\in S and x+a+b∉Sx+a+b\not\in S. Then H′H^{\prime} can be written as {y,y+a,y+b,y+a+b}\{y,~y+a,~y+b,~y+a+b\}. If y,y+a∈Sy,~y+a\in S then {x,x+a,y,y+a}\{x,~x+a,~y,~y+a\} is a [2,4][2,4]-flat, which is a contradiction. Similarly if y,y+b∈Sy,~y+b\in S we get a contradiction, and also if y+a,y+b∈Sy+a,~y+b\in S then we would have the [2,4][2,4]-flat {x+a,x+b,y+a,y+b}\{x+a,~x+b,~y+a,~y+b\}. So all in all, out of the points y,y+a,y+by,~y+a,~y+b at most one can be in SS, so H′H^{\prime} contains at most 2 points of SS and not 33, which is a contradiction. So the class cannot contain a [2,3][2,3]-flat different than HH. Summing up all points in the parallel class, we get that |S|≤5|S|\leq 5.

Any set of 44 points is contained in a 33-dimensional affine subspace, resolving the case |S|=4|S|=4. Finally if |S|=5|S|=5, then in the parallel class of HH, there must be a [2,2][2,2]-flat H′H^{\prime}. Letting H={x,x+a,x+b,x+a+b}H=\{x,~x+a,~x+b,~x+a+b\} with x,x+a,x+b∈Sx,~x+a,~x+b\in S and x+a+b∉Sx+a+b\not\in S, and H′={y,y+a,y+b,y+a+b}H^{\prime}=\{y,~y+a,~y+b,~y+a+b\}, one can easily see that no matter which two points of H′H^{\prime} are contained in SS, H∪H′H\cup H^{\prime} will always contain a [2,4][2,4]-flat induced by SS, which is a contradiction.

This concludes the proof that any SS with 4≤|S|≤2n−2−14\leq|S|\leq 2^{n-2}-1 induces a [3,4][3,4]-flat.

Now suppose that 4≤|S|≤2n−44\leq|S|\leq 2^{n}-4, and let us show that SS induces a [3,4][3,4]-flat. We use induction on nn. For n=3n=3, |S|=4|S|=4 so the whole space is a [3,4][3,4]-flat, while we have verified the case n=4n=4 via exhaustive search. From now on we assume that n≥5n\geq 5. The case 4≤|S|≤2n−2−14\leq|S|\leq 2^{n-2}-1 is already covered, and by Lemma 2.6, we are also done in the case 3⋅2n−2+1≤|S|≤2n−43\cdot 2^{n-2}+1\leq|S|\leq 2^{n}-4. Thus the remaining case is when 2n−2≤|S|≤3⋅2n−22^{n-2}\leq|S|\leq 3\cdot 2^{n-2} holds. By complementing, we can actually assume that 2n−2≤|S|≤2n−12^{n-2}\leq|S|\leq 2^{n-1}. We apply Lemma 2.2 of Charbit et al. [8] on SS, where either HH or H¯\overline{H} will be an n−1n-1-flat AA with |S∩A|∈[12​m,12​m+12​m]|S\cap A|\in\left[\frac{1}{2}m,\frac{1}{2}m+\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{m}\right]. Since m∈[2n−2,2n−1]m\in[2^{n-2},2^{n-1}], this means that |S∩A|∈[2n−3,2n−2+212​n−32]|S\cap A|\in\left[2^{n-3},2^{n-2}+2^{\frac{1}{2}n-\frac{3}{2}}\right]. Here n≥3n\geq 3 implies that 12​n−32≤n−3\frac{1}{2}n-\frac{3}{2}\leq n-3, so |S∩A|∈[2n−3,3⋅2n−3]|S\cap A|\in[2^{n-3},3\cdot 2^{n-3}]. Since n≥5n\geq 5, we have 2n−3≥42^{n-3}\geq 4 and 3⋅2n−3≤2n−1−43\cdot 2^{n-3}\leq 2^{n-1}-4, so |S∩A|∈[4,2n−1−4]|S\cap A|\in[4,2^{n-1}-4]. By the induction hypothesis, the statement is true in the n−1n-1-dimensional flat AA, so SS induces a [3,4][3,4]-flat in AA. ∎

Remark 2.10.

We have seen that S​p​(n,k,2k−1)=[2k−1,2n−2k−1]Sp(n;k,2^{k-1})=[2^{k-1},2^{n}-2^{k-1}] holds for k=1,2,3k=1,2,3. However this does not hold for larger kk. In fact, for k≥4k\geq 4 there does not exist a constant CC independent of nn such that [n,C]→[k,2k−1][n,C]\to[k,2^{k-1}] holds for all n≥kn\geq k, since for n≥max⁡(C−1,k+1)n\geq\max(C-1,k+1) we can pick a subset SS of size CC in general position, and then kk-flats only contain at most k+1k+1 points of SS while k+1<2k−1k+1<2^{k-1} for k≥4k\geq 4. As we will point out in Theorem 3.1 in the next section, even the (k,k+1)(k,k+1)-evasive sets can be exponentially large in nn.

3 Avoidable sizes with kk-dimensional subspaces

In this section, we show two types of constructions which have (several) missing values in their kk-dimensional profile. These in turn provide a relatively large set of missing values from the (n,k,t)(n;k,t)-spectrum. Moreover we point out that these constructions can be combined via disjoint union and difference, leading to even more missing values.

The first type corresponds to evasive sets, which were mentioned in the introduction. Here we refine the probabilistic bounds of Guruswami. Then we continue by constructing mm-sets which have a profile of relatively small size provided that mm has small support in its binary or in its canonical signed-digit binary representation.

3.1 Evasive sets

As we mentioned in the introduction, the existence of (k,c)(k,c)-evasive sets in turn provides sets which avoid every intersection size greater than cc. The random construction of Guruswami showed that we can obtain a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set on at least 2n⁡(1−2​kc)/2k+12^{n(1-\frac{2k}{c})}/2^{k+1} points. Below we refine his argument using alteration.

Theorem 3.1.

Let k,c∈ℤ+k,c\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} with c≥k+1c\geq k+1. Then for n>kn>k, there exists a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of size at least

⌊K⋅2n⁡(1−kc)⌋−1\lfloor K\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\rfloor-1

where K=K⁡(k,c):=cc+1⋅2k⁡(k+1)/c⋅(2​e2/3​(c+1)​(2kc+1))−1cK=K(k,c):=\frac{c}{c+1}\cdot 2^{k(k+1)/c}\cdot\left(2e^{2/3}(c+1)\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\right)^{-\frac{1}{c}}.

Proof.

To construct a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set, we apply the following procedure. First we suitably choose a value m∈[c,2n]m\in[c,2^{n}]. Then we take a random point set of size mm in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, and if we find a set of c+1c+1 points within a kk-flat, we erase one of those points.
Then the expected value of the number of erased points can be bounded from above by

2n−k​[nk]2​(2kc+1)​(2n−c−1m−c−1)(2nm)<2(n−k)​(k+1)+1​e2/3​(2kc+1)​(m2n)c+1.2^{n-k}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{2}\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\frac{\binom{{2^{n}}-c-1}{m-c-1}}{\binom{2^{n}}{m}}<2^{(n-k)(k+1)+1}e^{2/3}\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\left(\frac{m}{2^{n}}\right)^{c+1}.

Indeed, the probability that a given kk-flat contains at least c+1c+1 points of an mm-element random point set in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} is less than (2kc+1)​(2n−c−1m−c−1)(2nm)\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\frac{\binom{{2^{n}}-c-1}{m-c-1}}{\binom{2^{n}}{m}}, and we can apply the upper bound given in Lemma 2.5 on the number of kk-flats, which is 2n−k​[nk]22^{n-k}\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{2}, see Corollary 2.4.

The remaining points form a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set of size at least

m−2(n−k)​(k+1)+1​e2/3​(2kc+1)​(m2n)c+1m-2^{(n-k)(k+1)+1}e^{2/3}\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\left(\frac{m}{2^{n}}\right)^{c+1}

which we want to maximize in mm. Note that this is a concave function of mm, maximized when its derivative is 00. This happens when C⁡(n,k,c)​(c+1)​mc=1C(n,k,c)(c+1)m^{c}=1, where

C⁡(n,k,c):=2(n−k)​(k+1)+1​e2/3​(2kc+1)​(12n)c+1.C(n,k,c):=2^{(n-k)(k+1)+1}e^{2/3}\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\left(\frac{1}{2^{n}}\right)^{c+1}.

Hence the maximum of this function over ℝ\mathbb{R} is attained at

m=2n⁡(1−kc)⋅2k⁡(k+1)/c⋅(2​e2/3​(c+1)​(2kc+1))−1c,m=2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\cdot 2^{k(k+1)/c}\cdot\left(2e^{2/3}(c+1)\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\right)^{-\frac{1}{c}},

while the maximum itself is cc+1​m\frac{c}{c+1}m. As mm must be an integer, we get that the expected value is at least cc+1​m−1\frac{c}{c+1}m-1 for

m=⌊2n⁡(1−kc)⋅2k⁡(k+1)/c⋅(2​e2/3​(c+1)​(2kc+1))−1c⌋.m=\left\lfloor 2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\cdot 2^{k(k+1)/c}\cdot\left(2e^{2/3}(c+1)\binom{2^{k}}{c+1}\right)^{-\frac{1}{c}}\right\rfloor.

Note that the main term is 2n⁡(1−kc)2^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)} while its multiplicative factor is independent of nn, moreover using Stirling’s approximation on the constant, we can obtain that the number of remaining points is at least

2(n−k)​(1−kc)⋅c22​e​(c+1)−12^{(n-k)(1-\frac{k}{c})}\cdot\frac{c^{2}}{2e(c+1)}-1

for c≥k+1≥2.c\geq k+1\geq 2. This result refines the Theorem 1.1 of Guruswami. ∎

Remark 3.2.

Note that in the case c≤kc\leq k, any set of c+1c+1 points is contained in a cc-flat thus a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set can not contain more than cc points. However, for c>kc>k we already have an exponential lower bound on the size of (k,c)(k,c)-evasive sets in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}.

If q>2q>2, the same proof confirms the following generalization. The only difference is that we have a different constant for the bound on [nk]q\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{q} compared to [nk]2\begin{bmatrix}n\\ k\end{bmatrix}_{2} in Lemma 2.5.

Theorem 3.3 (General improved lower bound on evasive sets).

Let k,c∈ℤ+k,c\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} with c≥k+1c\geq k+1 and q>2q>2. Then for n>kn>k, there exists a (k,c)(k,c)-evasive set in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n} of size at least

⌊K⋅qn⁡(1−kc)⌋−1,\lfloor K\cdot q^{n\left(1-\frac{k}{c}\right)}\rfloor-1,

where K=K⁡(k,c):=cc+1⋅2k⁡(k+1)/c⋅(2​e1/(q−2)​(c+1)​(qkc+1))−1cK=K(k,c):=\frac{c}{c+1}\cdot 2^{k(k+1)/c}\cdot\left(2e^{1/(q-2)}(c+1)\binom{q^{k}}{c+1}\right)^{-\frac{1}{c}}.

3.2 Sets related to binary and canonical signed-digit representations

To prove Theorem 1.5, we will use the following construction.

Definition 3.4.

Let m∈[0,2n]m\in[0,2^{n}] be an integer. The lexicographic construction of mm points is defined as follows. Take every point P=(xn−1,xn−2,…,x0)P=(x_{n-1},x_{n-2},\ldots,x_{0}) in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} for which the nn-digit binary representation xn−1​xn−2​…​x0¯\overline{x_{n-1}x_{n-2}\ldots x_{0}} represents a number smaller than mm.
The lexicographic construction of mm points will be denoted by ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m}. The binary support Supp⁡(m)\mathrm{Supp}(m) of mm is the set of values d≥0d\geq 0 such that the binary form of mm contains a digit 1 at the place 2d2^{d}.
Finally, let s2​(m):=|Supp​(m)|s_{2}(m):=|\mathrm{Supp}(m)|, i.e., the sum of the digits in the binary representation of mm.

The following lemma is a straightforward consequence of the summation procedure, taking into account the decrease of the digit sum at each carry.

Lemma 3.5.

For any natural numbers a1a_{1}, a2a_{2}, …, aℓa_{\ell} we have s2​(∑i=1ℓai)≤∑i=1ℓs2​(ai)s_{2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}s_{2}(a_{i}).

Proposition 3.6.

If s2​(t)>s2​(m)s_{2}(t)>s_{2}(m) then [n,m]↛[k,t][n,m]\not\to[k,t], and in particular, ℒm⊆𝔽2n\mathcal{L}_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} does not induce a [k,t][k,t]-flat. Moreover, if HH is a kk-flat in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, then the size of H∩ℒmH\cap\mathcal{L}_{m} can admit at most

1+∑j=0s2​(m)(kj)1+\sum_{j=0}^{s_{2}(m)}\binom{k}{j}

values.

Proof.

Let M=s2​(m)M=s_{2}(m), and let m=∑i=1M2dim=\sum_{i=1}^{M}2^{d_{i}}, thus Supp(m)={d1<d2<…<dM}\mathrm{Supp}(m)=\{d_{1}<d_{2}<\ldots<d_{M}\}. Then ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m} naturally decomposes into MM flats H1,H2,…,HMH_{1},H_{2},\ldots,H_{M} of dimension d1,…,dMd_{1},\ldots,d_{M}, respectively, where the flat HjH_{j} of dimension djd_{j} is given by the equations

xk={1for ​k>dj,k∈Supp⁡(m)0for ​k>dj,k∉Supp⁡(m)0for ​k=dj.x_{k}=\begin{cases}1&\text{for }k>d_{j},k\in\mathrm{Supp}(m)\\ 0&\text{for }k>d_{j},k\not\in\mathrm{Supp}(m)\\ 0&\text{for }k=d_{j}.\end{cases}

Denote dim(H∩Hi)\dim(H\cap H_{i}) by rir_{i}. The size of H∩ℒmH\cap\mathcal{L}_{m} can be expressed as

∑i:Hi∩H≠∅2ri.\sum_{i:H_{i}\cap H\neq\emptyset}2^{r_{i}}.

Since the sets H∩HiH\cap H_{i} are disjoint subsets of HH and of ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m}, we conclude the sum above is at most min⁡{2k,m}\min\{2^{k},m\}. Moreover, if the sum is smaller than 2k2^{k}, then the binary representation of the sum consists of at most kk digits, of which at most MM is one, in view of Lemma 3.5. Taking into account the possibility |H∩ℒm|=2k|H\cap\mathcal{L}_{m}|=2^{k} as well, this completes the proof. ∎

Theorem 1.5 follows immediately from Proposition 3.6.

Not only the binary digit sum can impose conditions on the spectrum: the lexicographic construction shows further values of mm for which [k,t][k,t]-flats are avoidable. Suppose that mm is a difference of two powers of 22. While s2​(m)s_{2}(m) might be large, the lexicographic construction of mm points shows that [k,t][k,t] is avoidable if tt cannot be written as a power of 22 or a difference of two powers of 22. It is easy to deduce a statement similar to Proposition 3.6, after recalling the definition and the properties of the canonical signed-digit binary representation.

Let s2∗​(m)s^{*}_{2}(m) denote the number of nonzero values in the non-adjacent form or canonical signed-digit (CSD) binary representation of mm. This number system is a signed-digit number system using three digits, 0,1,1¯0,1,\overline{1}, which minimizes the number of non-zero digits. 1¯\overline{1} corresponds to −1-1. Its main advantage compared to the binary form is that CSD reduces the number of operations in a hardware multiplier. A detailed discussion of CSD can be found in [24]. We apply the following facts concerning this numerical system.

Proposition 3.7.

  • •

    The CSD representation of any integer number can be gained easily from the binary form by iterating the following step: starting from the right, going left, each sequence of length at least 33 consisting of a single 00 in the first position of the sequence and continued solely by 11s are replaced by a sequence of the same length, starting with 1, ending with 1¯\overline{1} and containing only 00 in between.

  • •

    The CSD representation of any integer number is unique.

  • •

    There are no two consecutive non-zero digits in the CSD representation of any integer number. Moreover, finite sequences built up by starting with a digit 11 or 1¯\overline{1} (as the leftmost digit) and continuing with zero or more blocks of the form 00, 0101, or 0​1¯0\overline{1} correspond uniquely to the nonzero integers via the CSD representation.

  • •

    For every integer nn, the CSD representation contains the least number of nonzero digits compared to any signed-digit binary representation of nn.

Table 1 presents the CSD representation of the first few positive integers. Note that the digits of the CSD form of mm correspond to the coefficients of the powers of 22 when m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} is written (uniquely) as m=∑iαi​2dim=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}2^{d_{i}} such that αi∈{±1}\alpha_{i}\in\{\pm 1\} for all ii and no pair of consecutive positive integers appears in the set of exponents of 22, i.e., |di−dj|≠1|d_{i}-d_{j}|\neq 1 for all pairs i,ji,j.

We have an analogue of Lemma 3.5 for the CSD binary representation, which follows easily from the last property of the CSD representation, formulated above.

Lemma 3.8.

For any integer numbers a1a_{1}, a2a_{2}, …, aℓa_{\ell} we have s2∗​(∑i=1ℓai)≤∑i=1ℓs2∗​(ai)s_{2}^{*}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}a_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}s_{2}^{*}(a_{i}).

The CSD representation offers a convenient tool to exclude further values from the spectra S​p​(n,k,t).Sp(n;k,t).

Proposition 3.9.

If s2∗​(t)>s2∗​(m)s^{*}_{2}(t)>s^{*}_{2}(m) then [n,m]↛[k,t][n,m]\not\to[k,t].

Proof.

The proof follows that of Proposition 3.6. Take the CSD representation m=∑i=1Mαi​2dim=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\alpha_{i}2^{d_{i}} with d1<d2<…<dMd_{1}<d_{2}<...<d_{M} and αi∈{±1}\alpha_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}. We will now provide a construction of ℒm⊆𝔽2n\mathcal{L}_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} according to this CSD form. For each 1≤j≤M+11\leq j\leq M+1, let mj=∑i=jMαi​2dim_{j}=\sum_{i=j}^{M}\alpha_{i}2^{d_{i}}. (Note that m1=mm_{1}=m and mM+1=0m_{M+1}=0.) Then one can obtain ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m} by starting from ℒmj=∅\mathcal{L}_{m_{j}}=\emptyset for j=M+1j=M+1, and for each j=M,M−1,…,1j=M,M-1,...,1 in turn, building ℒmj\mathcal{L}_{m_{j}} from ℒmj+1\mathcal{L}_{m_{j+1}}. 3.3 Combination

The propositions above can be combined with the former results on (k,c)(k,c)-evasive sets. Indeed, consider a lexicographic construction ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m} which avoids [k,t][k,t]-flats for all t∈[t1,t2]t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]. Take a (k,c)(k,c)-subspace evasive set SS disjoint from ℒm\mathcal{L}_{m}. Then ℒm∪S\mathcal{L}_{m}\cup S provides a set of size m+|S|m+|S| which avoids [k,t][k,t]-flats for all t∈[t1+c,t2]t\in[t_{1}+c,t_{2}].

4 Avoiding intersection sizes equal to a power of 22

In the previous section, we proved that [k,t][k,t]-flats are easier to avoid if the binary representation of tt contains many digits equal to 11. Here we discuss the case when s2​(t)s_{2}(t) is 11 or 22. The cornerstone will be a simple theorem which states that if a subset of 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} contains a large proportion of the vectors of the space then it must contain a large affine subspace as well.

4.1 Finding [k,2k][k,2^{k}]-flats

We will first consider the case of t=2kt=2^{k}, which means that we want to find a full affine subspace of dimension kk in SS. Recall that in Section 2, we have discussed the cases k=1k=1 and k=2k=2, with the case k=2k=2 corresponding to Sidon sets. The following theorem extends the result of Bose and Ray-Chaudhuri, presented in Proposition 2.8(i).

Theorem 4.1.

Given integers n≥k≥1n\geq k\geq 1, and any m≥52⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)m\geq\frac{5}{2}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}, we have [n,m]→[k,2k][n,m]\to[k,2^{k}].

The result points out that for a fixed integer kk, sets with given positive density will always contain a kk-flat if nn is large enough. We mention that the result and its proof is closely related to Szemerédi’s Cube Lemma, see [26, Corollary 2.1]. The statement of Theorem 4.1 follows from the work of Bonin and Qin [5]. We present a proof as it will be referred to during the proofs of the main results of the chapter.

Lemma 4.2.

Suppose that |S|≥D⋅2α​n+1|S|\geq D\cdot 2^{\alpha n}+1 for a set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, where 12≤α<1\frac{1}{2}\leq\alpha<1 and D>0D>0 are real numbers. Then there exists a nonzero vector d∈𝔽2nd\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} such that the number of unordered pairs of vectors in SS with difference dd is at least D22⋅2(2​α−1)​n\frac{D^{2}}{2}\cdot 2^{(2\alpha-1)n}.

Proof.

Taking the elements of SS pairwise, they form (|S|2)\binom{|S|}{2} differences with multiplicity. The number of possible differences is 2n−12^{n}-1, so there must exist a difference appearing at least

(|S|2)2n−1>(|S|2)2n≥D2⋅22​α​n2n+1=D22⋅2(2​α−1)​n\frac{\binom{|S|}{2}}{2^{n}-1}>\frac{\binom{|S|}{2}}{2^{n}}\geq\frac{D^{2}\cdot 2^{2\alpha n}}{2^{n+1}}=\frac{D^{2}}{2}\cdot 2^{(2\alpha-1)n}

times. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We prove that there exist constants 0<Ck≤520<C_{k}\leq\frac{5}{2} for each k≥1k\geq 1 such that if |S|⊆𝔽2n|S|\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} has |S|≥Ck⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)|S|\geq C_{k}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)} then SS contains a kk-flat. For k=1k=1, the result holds with C1=2C_{1}=2, as any two points form a 11-flat.

Now suppose that k≥2k\geq 2. If we know that |S|≥Dk⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)+1|S|\geq D_{k}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}+1 for a certain constant Dk>0D_{k}>0, then we can apply Lemma 4.2 to get a difference d1d_{1} which appears at least Dk22⋅2n⁡(1−12k−2)\frac{D_{k}^{2}}{2}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)} times. We factorize the space by this vector and define a set S1⊆𝔽2n/⟨d1⟩S_{1}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}/\langle d_{1}\rangle which consists of the ⟨d1⟩\langle d_{1}\rangle-cosets with both elements lying in SS. Then |S1|≥Dk22⋅2n⁡(1−12k−2)|S_{1}|\geq\frac{D_{k}^{2}}{2}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)}.

Observe that if we find a [k−1,2k−1][k-1,2^{k-1}]-flat induced by S1S_{1}, then it can be lifted to a [k,2k][k,2^{k}]-flat induced by SS. So to find such a (k−1)(k-1)-flat and finish the proof, it suffices to refer to the induction hypothesis for the subset S1S_{1} of the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional space 𝔽2n/⟨d1⟩\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}/\langle d_{1}\rangle. For this, it suffices to have Dk22⋅2n⁡(1−12k−2)≥Ck−1⋅2(n−1)​(1−12k−2)\frac{D_{k}^{2}}{2}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)}\geq C_{k-1}\cdot 2^{(n-1)\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-2}}\right)}.

This is equivalent to Dk≥Ck−1⋅212k−1D_{k}\geq\sqrt{C_{k-1}}\cdot 2^{\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}}, so we need a value CkC_{k} such that Ck⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)≥Ck−1⋅212k−1⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)+1C_{k}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}\geq\sqrt{C_{k-1}}\cdot 2^{\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}}\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}+1 holds for all n≥kn\geq k. The choice Ck=Ck−1⋅212k−1+12k⁡(1−12k−1)C_{k}=\sqrt{C_{k-1}}\cdot 2^{\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}}+\frac{1}{2^{k\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)}} works.

From C1=2C_{1}=2 this gives C2=52C_{2}=\frac{5}{2}, and for k≥3k\geq 3, if we already know that Ck−1≤52C_{k-1}\leq\frac{5}{2} then we will get Ck≤52⋅21/4+123​(1−122)≈2.09<52C_{k}\leq\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}\cdot 2^{1/4}+\frac{1}{2^{3\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{2}}\right)}}\approx 2.09<\frac{5}{2}. ∎

Remark 4.3.

In fact, in the argument above the recursive formula gives Ck→1C_{k}\to 1 as k→∞k\to\infty. From this argument one can also deduce that for each fixed k≥1k\geq 1 and δ>0\delta>0, |S|≥(2+δ)⋅2n⁡(1−12k−1)|S|\geq(2+\delta)\cdot 2^{n\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{k-1}}\right)} already implies the existence of a [k,2k][k,2^{k}]-flat for sufficiently large nn.

We recall the statement of Theorem 1.9.

The following theorem is a more specific form of Theorem 1.8:

Theorem 4.5.

We continue our investigation for the case when the binary form of tt contains exactly two 11s which are consecutive. The main focus will be the proof of Theorem 1.10, which we will recall:

Theorem 1.10. For every pair (k,ℓ)(k,\ell) of integers with 2≤ℓ≤k−12\leq\ell\leq k-1, the density of integer values mm within the interval [0,12ℓ−1⋅2n]\left[0,\frac{1}{2^{\ell-1}}\cdot 2^{n}\right] for which [n,m]→[k,3⋅2k−ℓ][n,m]\to[k,3\cdot 2^{k-\ell}] holds, tends to 11 as n→∞n\to\infty. The proof builds on ideas similar to those used for Theorem 4.5, this time bounding the number of [2,3][2,3]-flats in SS based on its additive energy, which is an additive combinatorial notion that we will now define.

For a set S⊆𝔽2nS\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, let the additive energy of SS (a notion introduced by Tao and Vu [28, Section 2.3]), denoted by E⁡(S)E(S) be as follows:

E⁡(S)={(u1,u2,u3,u4)∈S4:u1+u2=u3+u4}.E(S)=\{(u_{1},u_{2},u_{3},u_{4})\in S^{4}:u_{1}+u_{2}=u_{3}+u_{4}\}.

However, this can only happen if mm is a power of 22.

In fact, the bound E⁡(S)≤m3E(S)\leq m^{3} can be improved in general using the concept below.

Definition 5.1.

For d∈ℤ+d\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} and a∈ℤa\in\mathbb{Z}, define the least absolute residue of aa modulo dd, denoted ra​(d)r_{a}(d), by

5.2 Bounding sizes of hypercube cuts

Definition 5.5.

The nn-dimensional hypercube graph QnQ_{n} is a graph with vertex set 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} such that two vertices are connected by an edge if and only if their Hamming distance is 1.

Definition 5.6.

Define the function Ψ:ℕ+→ℕ\Psi:\mathbb{N}^{+}\to\mathbb{N} by Ψ⁡(t)=∑i=0t−1s2​(i)\Psi(t)=\sum\limits_{i=0}^{t-1}s_{2}(i). Recall that s2s_{2} denotes the binary digit sum function.

Observe that for any positive integer kk we have Ψ⁡(2k)=k⋅2k−1\Psi(2^{k})=k\cdot 2^{k-1}, as for each 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, precisely half of the integers between 00 and 2k−12^{k}-1 have a digit 11 at the jthj^{\mathrm{th}} position in the binary representation.

Lemma 5.7 (Hart, [16]).

For a positive integer tt, let c⁡(t)c(t) be the maximum number of edges in a tt-vertex subgraph of QnQ_{n} ranging over all possible values n∈ℕ+n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. Then for each tt we have c⁡(t)≤Ψ⁡(t)c(t)\leq\Psi(t).

See [16] for a proof and a description of the subgraphs attaining the upper bound for c⁡(t)c(t). Notably, one such optimal subgraph is induced by the lexicographic construction ℒt\mathcal{L}_{t}, introduced in Definition 3.4. For any T⊆V⁡(Qn)T\subseteq V(Q_{n}) we have the simple relation

2​e​(T)+e⁡(T,T¯)=n​|T|2e(T)+e(T,\overline{T})=n|T|

by double counting all incident edges to each point of TT [16]. This yields the corollary below.

Corollary 5.8 (Hart, Theorem 1.5, [16]).

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and 1≤t≤2n−11\leq t\leq 2^{n}-1 be fixed integers. Then the minimum possible value of e⁡(T,T¯)e(T,\overline{T}) for a subset T⊆V⁡(Qn)T\subseteq V(Q_{n}) of size tt is n​t−2​Ψ​(t)nt-2\Psi(t).

From this, we derive the following consequence:

Proposition 5.9.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and 0≤d≤n−10\leq d\leq n-1 be integers. Take any cut T∪T¯=𝔽2nT\cup\overline{T}=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of the nn-dimensional hypercube graph QnQ_{n} that has at least 2d2^{d} points in both parts. Then at least 2d​(n−d)2^{d}(n-d) edges of QnQ_{n} cross the cut, i.e., e⁡(T,T¯)≥2d​(n−d)e(T,\overline{T})\geq 2^{d}(n-d).

Proof.

Suppose that t=|T|t=|T| and 2d≤t≤2n−12^{d}\leq t\leq 2^{n-1}. Using Corollary 5.8, we only need to show that n​t−2​Ψ​(t)≥2d​(n−d)nt-2\Psi(t)\geq 2^{d}(n-d) holds.

It is elementary to see that for integers 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1, the function 2k​(n−k)2^{k}(n-k) is increasing. This implies that in the case t=2n−1t=2^{n-1}, the statement holds as n​t−2​∑i=0t−1s2​(i)=n⋅2n−1−2​(n−1)​2n−2=2n−1=2n−1​(n−(n−1))≥2d​(n−d)nt-2\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}s_{2}(i)=n\cdot 2^{n-1}-2(n-1)2^{n-2}=2^{n-1}=2^{n-1}(n-(n-1))\geq 2^{d}(n-d).
So from now on, assume that 2d≤t<2n−12^{d}\leq t<2^{n-1}. The monotonicity implies that we can assume 2d≤t<2d+12^{d}\leq t<2^{d+1}, where d≤n−2d\leq n-2.

The function Ψ\Psi can be related to the well-known Takagi function τ\tau, which is a continuous but nowhere differentiable non-negative function on [0,1][0,1]. Let t∈ℤ+t\in\mathbb{Z}^{+} be expressed as t=2d​(1+x)t=2^{d}(1+x) for d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} and x∈[0,1)x\in[0,1). Then

2​Ψ​(t)=t​d+2d​(2​x−τ⁡(x)),2\Psi(t)=td+2^{d}(2x-\tau(x)), (2)

see Monroe [22, Corollary 5.0.8 (a)]. For a survey on the Takagi function, see [20].

Now n​t−2​Ψ​(t)≥2d​(n−d)⇔2​Ψ​(t)≤n⁡(t−2d)+d⋅2dnt-2\Psi(t)\geq 2^{d}(n-d)\Leftrightarrow 2\Psi(t)\leq n(t-2^{d})+d\cdot 2^{d}. Since n≥d+2n\geq d+2, it suffices to prove that 2​Ψ​(t)≤(d+2)​(t−2d)+d⋅2d2\Psi(t)\leq(d+2)(t-2^{d})+d\cdot 2^{d}. By (2), this is equivalent to

t​d+2d​(2​x−τ⁡(x))≤(d+2)​(t−2d)+d⋅2d⇔2d+1​x−2d⋅τ⁡(x)≤2⋅2d​x,td+2^{d}(2x-\tau(x))\leq(d+2)(t-2^{d})+d\cdot 2^{d}\Leftrightarrow 2^{d+1}x-2^{d}\cdot\tau(x)\leq 2\cdot 2^{d}x,

which holds since τ⁡(x)≥0\tau(x)\geq 0 for all xx. ∎

Let us prove a slightly different version of this proposition, for the case of multiple copies of the hypercube graph.

Proposition 5.10.

Let n≥1n\geq 1, k≥1k\geq 1 and 0≤d≤n−20\leq d\leq n-2 be integers. Let k​QnkQ_{n} denote the disjoint union of kk copies Qn(1)Q_{n}^{(1)}, Qn(2)Q_{n}^{(2)}, …, Qn(k)Q_{n}^{(k)} of the hypercube graph QnQ_{n}. By [16, Proposition 2.1], the function Ψ\Psi satisfies the recursion

Ψ⁡(t)=max0<m≤t2⁡(Ψ⁡(m)+Ψ⁡(t−m)+m),\Psi(t)=\max\limits_{0<m\leq\frac{t}{2}}(\Psi(m)+\Psi(t-m)+m),

hence for any partition t=t1+t2t=t_{1}+t_{2} with t1,t2∈ℤ+t_{1},t_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}, we have Ψ⁡(t)≥Ψ⁡(t1)+Ψ⁡(t2)\Psi(t)\geq\Psi(t_{1})+\Psi(t_{2}). In this case, each ii satisfies |Ai|<2d≤2n−2|A_{i}|<2^{d}\leq 2^{n-2}. Letting σj=∑i=1j|Ai|\sigma_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{j}|A_{i}| for each 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, we have σk=|A|≥2d\sigma_{k}=|A|\geq 2^{d}. Then σj−1<2d\sigma_{j-1}<2^{d}, and σj=σj−1+|Aj|<2d+2d≤2n−1\sigma_{j}=\sigma_{j-1}+|A_{j}|<2^{d}+2^{d}\leq 2^{n-1}. n​|A1|−2​Ψ​(|A1|)+n​|A2|−2​Ψ​(|A2|)+…+n|Aj|−2​Ψ​(|Aj|)≥n⁡(|A1|+|A2|+…+|Aj|)−2​Ψ​(|A1|+|A2|+…+|Aj|)=n​σj−2​Ψ​(σj)\begin{split}n|A_{1}|-2\Psi(|A_{1}|)+n|A_{2}|-2\Psi(|A_{2}|)+...+n|A_{j}|-2\Psi(|A_{j}|)\geq\\ n(|A_{1}|+|A_{2}|+...+|A_{j}|)-2\Psi(|A_{1}|+|A_{2}|+...+|A_{j}|)=n\sigma_{j}-2\Psi(\sigma_{j})\end{split} (3)

6 Concluding remarks

For general pairs (k,t)(k,t), it remained open to decide whether the density of the spectrum ρ⁡(n,k,t)=S​p​(n,k,t)2n\rho(n;k,t)=\frac{Sp(n;k,t)}{2^{n}} tends to 11 as nn tends to infinity, or even to obtain a general constant lower bound on this density for a given pair (k,t)(k,t) with 0≤t≤2k0\leq t\leq 2^{k}. The proof of Theorem 1.10 suggests that such a result might be deduced from a supersaturation type result on [k,t][k,t]-flats, similar to the lower bound on F2,3F_{2,3} derived from Proposition 5.2.

We did not elaborate on the case q>2q>2. However, note that the approach we used to exclude several values from the spectra S​p​(n,k,t)Sp(n;k,t) applies for q>2q>2 as well. Indeed, we can construct point sets as a combination of disjoint full flats and point sets which hit every kk-flat in small number of points, i.e., evasive sets. However, proving density results on the spectrum appear to be much harder, as it was the case even for q=3q=3 with lines (or full flats), as the general problem contains the determination of the order of magnitude of the maximum size of qq-AP-free sets of 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}.

While we focused on the sets in AG⁡(n,q)\mathrm{AG}(n,q), q=2q=2, we mention that the analogous question was investigated by Ihringer and Verstraëte [19] for point sets XX in a projective space PG⁡(n,q)\mathrm{PG}(n,q) where all kk-dimensional subspaces must have a bounded number of points. However their results concern the case when qq is large.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
